title: Balancing complete combustion: C, then H, then O

beats.text: In complete combustion, a fuel burns in plenty of oxygen, and all its carbon ends up as carbon dioxide and all its hydrogen as water. Let's balance the complete combustion of methanol, a fuel that already contains an oxygen atom.
Balance carbon first. Methanol has one carbon, so we need one carbon dioxide. The counters now match for carbon.
Next, hydrogen. Methanol has four hydrogen atoms: three on the carbon and one on the oxygen. Each water has two, so we need two water molecules.

Oxygen last, because oxygen gas is the only reactant we can adjust freely. The products now contain two oxygens in carbon dioxide plus two in the waters: four in total. Methanol already supplies one of them. So oxygen gas must supply the other three, which is one and a half oxygen molecules.

A half is fine in a thermochemical equation, but to get whole numbers, double everything: two methanol plus three oxygen gives two carbon dioxide plus four water. Check the counters: two carbons, eight hydrogens, eight oxygens on each side.
